name: Spirulina extract

card.summary: An extract of blue-green algae, rich in pigments such as phycocyanin, used in cosmetics and supplements for its antioxidant and anti-glycation properties that people link to healthier-looking skin.
card.note: Quality varies; contaminated batches of cyanobacteria supplements have been reported.

quick.overview:
Spirulina is a cyanobacterium (blue-green alga), now classed mainly as Limnospira or Arthrospira, eaten as a food and supplement and used as a colourant. Extracts concentrate particular fractions, such as the blue pigment-protein phycocyanin or immune-active lipoproteins.

For looks, spirulina extracts appear in skincare and supplement products aimed at skin health, with interest centred on antioxidant and anti-glycation activity, since glycation is one process linked to skin ageing. The human trials found so far study immune markers in athletes and healthy volunteers rather than skin appearance.
quick.how: Extracts are taken as oral supplements or included in topical cosmetic formulations, and phycocyanin is also used as a natural blue colourant. Published human studies used oral extract over days to weeks.
quick.risks: Wikipedia notes spirulina may interact with immune-affecting and blood-clotting medications, that some cyanobacteria produce microcystin toxins and contaminated batches can contain them, that heavy-metal contamination has been reported in some supplements, and that people with phenylketonuria should avoid it. Allergy is rare.

lead: Spirulina extract refers to preparations made from the cyanobacterium Arthrospira (Spirulina) platensis. The whole organism is a dried food and supplement with a long history, eaten by the Aztecs and by communities around Lake Chad[1]. Extracts isolate parts of it, including phycobiliproteins such as phycocyanin, which are used in food, medicine and cosmetics as pigments and bioactive ingredients[2][3].

The route to better-looking skin is through antioxidant and anti-glycation effects. A 2024 laboratory study reported that an aqueous spirulina extract had antiglycating effects on glucose-induced glycation of bovine serum albumin[4]. Glycation is one of the processes discussed in skin ageing, though that study did not measure skin.

Human trials have looked elsewhere. A randomised trial in 19 members of the Polish rowing team tested 1500 mg of extract for six weeks on immune cell responses to maximal exercise[5], and a pilot study of Immulina, an extract enriched for Braun-type lipoproteins, reported higher natural killer cell activity in healthy volunteers[6].

chain: Extract supplies antioxidant pigments such as phycocyanin
angle.text: Spirulina extracts are used in skincare and supplements for their antioxidant pigments and anti-glycation activity, which people connect to skin that looks healthier and ages more slowly.

infobox: C-phycocyanin absorbs light near 621 nm; water-soluble blue pigment-protein[9]
Genus renamed several times; current research places it in Limnospira[1]

paras: Cosmetic and appearance uses: spirulina-derived pigments and extracts feature in reviews of natural colourants for food, cosmetics and pharmaceutical applications[3][2]. Skincare products and supplements market them for antioxidant support.
Other uses: as a food, a supplement, and a feed ingredient in aquaculture and poultry[1].

Phycocyanin as a colourant: C-phycocyanin is a water-soluble blue pigment-protein that cyanobacteria use to harvest light, and it is sold as a natural blue food colourant in products such as sweets and ice cream. Wikipedia notes it holds its colour poorly at high heat unless stabilised, so it suits low-temperature preparations; laboratory studies report radical-scavenging and anti-inflammatory activity, which Wikipedia describes as preliminary.[9]

Wikipedia says the Aztecs ate spirulina, called tecuitlatl, from Lake Texcoco in Mexico until the 16th century, and that a soldier with Cortes described it sold as cakes.[1] In 1940 Pierre Dangeard described dihe, a spirulina cake eaten by the Kanembu people near Lake Chad, and botanist Jean Leonard confirmed in 1964-1965 that dihe is spirulina; growth studies in the 1970s laid the groundwork for large-scale production.[1] Today it is cultivated worldwide, mostly in open raceway ponds, and grows best at a pH near 8.5 or higher and about 30 degrees C.[1]

Dried spirulina is about 57 percent protein with B vitamins and minerals such as iron and manganese[1]. Wikipedia says it lacks reliable vitamin B12, containing mainly pseudovitamin B12 that is inactive in humans[1]. Phycobilins and phycobiliproteins are the pigments used in food and medicine[2]. Per 100 g dried, Wikipedia gives roughly 290 kcal, 24 g carbohydrate and 8 g fat, with thiamine and riboflavin well above 100 percent of the daily value and iron around 158 percent.[1]

Laboratory work includes the anti-glycation study[4] and a study on age-induced vascular dysfunction[7]. Wikipedia reports that the US NIH says evidence is insufficient to recommend spirulina for any human condition, and that the EFSA rejected diabetes-related claims in 2013[1]. The same article says studies in people with HIV found no conclusive effect on mortality, body weight or immune response.[1]

Wikipedia lists possible interactions with immune and clotting drugs, microcystin and heavy-metal contamination in some batches, and avoidance by people with phenylketonuria[1]. Wikipedia adds that spirulina itself does not make microcystins but contaminated batches can; microcystin exposure can cause gastrointestinal upset, chronic exposure may harm the liver, and children and pregnant women are considered especially vulnerable. Health Canada's 2016 review found varying microcystin levels and set a limit for microcystin-LR in finished products, Chinese regulators reported widespread lead, mercury and arsenic in spirulina sold there, and five allergy cases, four of them anaphylaxis, had been reported through July 2023.[1] Doses of 10 to 19 g per day for several months have been used safely in studies, according to the same page.[1]

No studies found examining spirulina extract for skin appearance. Human studies include a randomised double-blind trial in 19 rowers on immune cell responses[5], a pilot and crossover study of Immulina on natural killer cell markers in healthy volunteers[6], and a randomised placebo-controlled study of spirulina extract with zinc in chronic arsenic poisoning[8].
